The Salt Satyagraha (1930) was a direct challenge to the Salt Act of 1882. The British government held a monopoly on salt production and imposed a tax on it. Mahatma Gandhi chose salt as the symbol of protest because it was a daily necessity for everyone, linking the movement to the poorest Indians. This act marked the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement.

Further Insights:

Dandi March Statistics

· Dates: 12 March 1930 - 6 April 1930 (24 Days).

· Route: Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi (Gujarat).

· Distance: ~240 miles (~385 km).

· Volunteers: Gandhi + 78 members.

Regional Leaders of Salt Satyagraha

Different leaders led similar marches across India simultaneously:

RegionLeaderKey Fact
Tamil NaduC. RajagopalachariVedaranyam March (Trichy to Vedaranyam).
KeralaK. KelappanKnown as "Kerala Gandhi"; marched to Payyanur.
PeshawarKhan Abdul Ghaffar KhanLed 'Red Shirts' (Khudai Khidmatgars).
DharasanaSarojini NaiduLed the raid on salt works (Imam Saheb accompanied).
ManipurRani GaidinliuLed revolt against British in Naga hills at age 13.

Key Outcomes

· Journalist: American journalist Webb Miller covered the Dharasana beatings, gaining global sympathy.

· Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931): Signed on March 5, 1931. The movement was suspended, and Gandhi agreed to attend the 2nd Round Table Conference.

The Government of India appointed Prof. Rajeeva Laxman Karandikar as the Chairperson (part-time) of the National Statistical Commission (NSC) in December 2022.

· Background: He is a Professor Emeritus at the Chennai Mathematical Institute (CMI).

· Specialization: He is a renowned mathematician and statistician, widely known for his work in psephology (scientific study of elections/opinion polls) and probability theory.

· Tenure: The appointment was made for a period of three years.

Further Insights:

Formation & Mandate

· Established: 12th July 2006.

· Recommendation: Based on the C. Rangarajan Commission (2001) report.

· Objective: To reduce data problems and improve the credibility of official statistics in India.

· Status: It is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI).

Composition

The Commission consists of a Chairperson and four Members.

PositionStatus/Details
ChairpersonAppointed by the Central Govt (Status of Minister of State).
Members (4)Experts in Statistics (Status of Secretary to GoI).
Ex-officio MemberCEO, NITI Aayog.
SecretaryChief Statistician of India (CSI) serves as the Secretary.

Key Personalities

· First Chairman: Prof. Suresh D. Tendulkar (2006 - 2009).

· Current Chairman: Prof. Rajeeva Laxman Karandikar (Appointed 2022).

· Chief Statistician of India: The Secretary of MoSPI acts as the CSI (currently Saurabh Garg, IAS).

Important Function:

· National Statistical Day: Celebrated on 29th June (Birthday of P.C. Mahalanobis, the father of Indian Statistics).

Under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023 (which replaces Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act), electronic evidence is admissible only if authenticated.

· The Requirement: A Certificate is mandatory to prove the source and integrity of the electronic record.

· Digital Signature/Hash: The Act (via its Schedule) requires the certificate to contain the Hash Value (a cryptographic digital fingerprint) or digital signature to prove that the file has not been tampered with.

Further Insights:

Key Legal Shift:

The BSA replaces the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 to modernize evidence rules.

FeatureOld Act (IEA 1872)New Act (BSA 2023)
Electronic RecordsTreated as Secondary Evidence (usually).Treated as "Documents" (Can be Primary Evidence).
AdmissibilitySection 65B Certificate.Section 63 Certificate.
AuthenticationBasic verification by user.Verification by Expert + Hash Value.

What is Section 63?

· It is the specific section dealing with the admissibility of electronic records.

· Strict Standard: A certificate must be signed by the person in charge of the computer AND an expert to verify that the "Hash Value" matches the original data.

Expanded Definitions

The definition of "Document" in the new Act now explicitly covers:

· Server logs & Location data.

· Emails & Voice mails.

· Data stored in semiconductor memory (USB drives, SD cards).

Bisht Doab is the land between the Beas and the Sutlej rivers.

The name "Bisht" is derived from the first letters of its rivers: Beas + Sutlej = Bisht.

Further Insights:

The word "Punjab" means "Land of Five Rivers" (Panj = Five, Ab = Water). The land between any two rivers is called a "Doab".

Key Geography Note:

· These Doabs are part of the Indus River System.

· Sutlej is the southernmost river; Indus is the westernmost/northernmost.

Article 263 of the Constitution empowers the President of India to establish an Inter-State Council to investigate and discuss subjects of common interest between the Union and the States, or among the States themselves.

· Purpose: To effect coordination between States and the Centre.

· Key Fact: It is a Constitutional Body (unlike Zonal Councils).

Further Insights:

· Establishment: The Inter-State Council was set up in 1990 based on the recommendations of the Sarkaria Commission.

· Chairman: The Prime Minister.

· Composition:

o Prime Minister (Chairman)

o Chief Ministers of all States & UTs (with assemblies)

o Administrators of UTs (without assemblies)

o 6 Central Cabinet Ministers (nominated by PM)

· Comparison with Zonal Councils:

o Inter-State Council: Constitutional (Art. 263).

o Zonal Councils: Statutory (Established under States Reorganisation Act, 1956).

India's first Green Hydrogen Hub is being established in Pudimadaka (near Visakhapatnam), Andhra Pradesh.

· Key Developer: It is being developed by NTPC Green Energy Limited (NGEL).

· Significance: This is the first dedicated Green Hydrogen Hub under the National Green Hydrogen Mission.

· Foundation: The foundation stone was laid by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in January 2025.

Further Insights:

· The Goal: India aims to produce 5 million Metric Tonnes (MMT) of Green Hydrogen per year by 2030.

· The Process: Green Hydrogen is produced by splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using an Electrolyzer powered by renewable energy (Solar/Wind).

· Why Pudimadaka? The location was chosen for its proximity to the coast (access to seawater for electrolysis) and existing port infrastructure for exports.

· Investment: The project involves an investment of approximately ₹1.85 lakh crore over several phases.

Many Kushana rulers adopted the title "Devaputra" (Son of God) to claim divine status and legitimize their rule.

· Inspiration: This title was likely inspired by the Chinese practice where emperors called themselves the "Son of Heaven."

· Purpose: It was a political tool to show that their authority was derived directly from the gods.

Further Insights:

· The Kushanas ruled large parts of North India and Central Asia.

Founder: Kujula Kadphises.

· Most Famous Ruler: Kanishka (ruled c. 78 AD - 105 AD).

· Capitals:

1) Purushapura (Modern Peshawar, Pakistan) - Primary capital.

2) Mathura (India) - Second capital.

· Kanishka's Achievements:

· Started the Shaka Era (78 AD), which is used by the Government of India.

· Organized the 4th Buddhist Council in Kashmir (Kundalavana).

· Patronized scholars like Ashvaghosha (author of Buddhacharita), Charaka (father of Ayurveda), and Nagarjuna.

Gold Coins: The Kushanas were the first to issue gold coins on a large scale in India with high purity.

Ippon: The highest score in Judo. It signifies a decisive victory (like a knockout), ending the match immediately.

Hansoku-make: A grave penalty (disqualification). If a player receives this, the match ends immediately, and the opponent wins.

Other options:

· (1) Shime-waza are choking techniques. (Arm locks are Kansetsu-waza).

· (4) Hansoku-make is a major penalty (DQ). Minor penalties are called Shido.

Further Insights:

Founder: Jigoro Kano (Japan, 1882).

Uniform: Judogi.

Scoring System:

· Ippon: Immediate Win (Full point).

· Waza-ari: Half point (Two Waza-ari = Ippon).

Penalties:

· Shido: Minor penalty (warning). 3 Shidos = Hansoku-make.

· Hansoku-make: Disqualification (Direct loss).

Technique Categories:

· Nage-waza: Throwing techniques.

· Katame-waza: Grappling (Ground) techniques.

· Kansetsu-waza: Joint locks (Only elbow locks are allowed in competition).

· Shime-waza: Choking techniques.

The National IPR Policy (2016) was adopted to create a vibrant intellectual property ecosystem in India. Its first objective is specifically focused on raising awareness.

The policy lists 7 Key Objectives:

Objective No.Focus AreaGoal
1IPR AwarenessCreate public awareness about the benefits of IPRs.
2Generation of IPRsStimulate the creation of IPRs (encourage filing).
3Legal FrameworkHave strong, effective laws consistent with international pacts.
4AdministrationModernize and digitize IPR offices.
5CommercializationGet value for IPRs through commercialization.
6EnforcementStrengthen mechanisms against counterfeiting/piracy.
7Human CapitalExpand resources for teaching, training, and research in IPR.

Further Insights:

Policy Basics:

· Adopted: May 2016.

· Tagline: "Creative India; Innovative India" (Rachnatmak Bharat; Abhinav Bharat).

· Nodal Agency: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce.

· CIPAM: Cell for IPR Promotion and Management (CIPAM) was created to implement this policy.

Important IPR Acts & Tenures:

Different types of Intellectual Property have different validity periods in India.

IPR TypeGoverning ActTerm of Protection (Validity)
PatentThe Patents Act, 197020 Years
TrademarkTrade Marks Act, 199910 Years (Renewable indefinitely)
CopyrightCopyright Act, 195760 Years (Lifetime of author + 60 years)
DesignDesigns Act, 200010 Years (Extendable by 5 years)
GI TagGI of Goods Act, 199910 Years (Renewable)

International Treaties (India is a member):

· WIPO: World Intellectual Property Organization (Headquarters: Geneva, Switzerland).

· TRIPS: Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (WTO agreement).

· Budapest Treaty: Related to deposits of microorganisms for patent procedures.

· Berne Convention: Related to Copyrights.

· Paris Convention: Related to Industrial Property (Patents, Trademarks).

Babur's first expedition into India took place in 1519, during which he conquered Bajaur and Bhira (located on the banks of the river Jhelum).Before the famous Battle of Panipat (1526), Babur made four preliminary expeditions to test India's defenses. Bhira was the first significant conquest, which he claimed as his own by right of his ancestor Timur.

Further Insights:

·

Total Expeditions: Babur led 5 expeditions into India.

· First Use of Gunpowder: Babur used artillery and gunpowder for the first time in the attack on Bajaur/Bhira (1519), contrary to the popular belief that it was first used at Panipat.

· The "Big 4" Battles:

i. Panipat (1526): Defeated Ibrahim Lodi (Foundation of Mughal Empire).

ii. Khanwa (1527): Defeated Rana Sanga (Assumed title Ghazi).

iii. Chanderi (1528): Defeated Medini Rai.

iv. Ghagra (1529): Defeated the Afghans (Mahmud Lodi).

· War Tactics: Famous for Tulughma (flanking maneuver) and Araba (carts tied together) used at Panipat.

· Autobiography: Tuzuk-i-Baburi (Baburnama) written in Chaghatai Turkish.

In the Jhora dance, participants (both men and women) form a circle and hold each other's arms (interlinking them) to maintain the chain while moving with synchronized steps.

Further Insights:

· State: Uttarakhand (Kumaon Region) & parts of Himachal Pradesh.

· Occasion: Performed during Spring (Holi/Baisakhi) and weddings.

· Key Instrument: Hurka (a traditional drum).

· Social Significance: It is a community dance that breaks caste barriers; people of all castes join the circle together.

· Formation: Can be a single circle or "Do Manjila Jhora" (double-story/tiered circle) if the crowd is large.

· The Kumaon Mandal Vikas Nigam (Govt of Uttarakhand) specifically describe the dance as "dancers dance in a circle by holding each other's arms."

· While some similar circle dances (like Nati or Chanchari) may sometimes involve holding wrists or shoulders depending on the region, the standard definition for Jhora is linking arms.

In the 2008 Beijing Olympics, Sushil Kumar lost his opening bout to Andriy Stadnik (Ukraine). However, because Stadnik reached the final, Sushil got a second chance via the Repechage system.

· He won three consecutive bouts in the repechage rounds (defeating wrestlers from the USA, Switzerland, and Kazakhstan) to clinch the Bronze medal.

· This ended India's 56-year drought in Olympic wrestling (since K.D. Jadhav in 1952).

Further Insights:

· Double Medalist: Sushil Kumar was the first Indian to win two individual Olympic medals (Bronze in 2008, Silver in 2012).

· 2012 London: He won Silver, becoming the first Indian wrestler to reach an Olympic final.

· Repechage Rule: A rule in combat sports (Wrestling/Judo) allowing players who lose to the finalists to fight for a Bronze medal.

· Other Key Wrestlers:

i. K.D. Jadhav: First individual medalist (Bronze, 1952).

ii. Sakshi Malik: First female wrestling medalist (Bronze, 2016).

iii. Ravi Dahiya: Second wrestler to win Silver (2020 Tokyo).

Statement 1 (Wrong): "Slow and steady" expansion (Quasi-static) produces the maximum work. "Sudden" expansion (Irreversible) wastes energy, so the work done is less, not greater.

Statement 2 (Correct): For an ideal engine (Carnot engine), efficiency depends only on the temperature difference between the hot source and the cold sink.

Statement 3 (Correct): Heat naturally flows from Hot to Cold. To make it go from Cold to Hot (like in a Refrigerator), you must use external energy (electricity/work).

Further Insights:

· First Law: Energy cannot be created or destroyed (Law of Conservation of Energy).

· Second Law: Heat cannot flow from Cold to Hot without a machine (like a fridge).

· Carnot Engine: The most efficient theoretical engine possible.

· Entropy: A measure of "disorder." The disorder of the universe is always increasing.

The Global Firepower (GFP) ranking uses a complex formula involving over 60 individual factors to determine a nation's PowerIndex (PwrIndx) score.

· Not just weapons: It looks at manpower, equipment, finances, geography, and natural resources.

· The Goal: To assess a nation's potential conventional war-making capability across land, sea, and air.

Further Insights:

· Top 4 Powers:

1) USA

2) Russia

3) China

4) India

· The Score: The perfect score is 0.0000. The lower the score, the more powerful the military.

· Nuclear weapons: The index focuses on conventional warfare. While nuclear stockpiles are acknowledged (often as a bonus), the ranking does not rely solely on them.

· Landlocked Countries: They are not penalized for lacking a navy.

· Rocket: PSLV-C11

· Key Achievement: It dropped the Moon Impact Probe (MIP) on the lunar surface and confirmed the existence of water.

Gaganyaan is India's first human spaceflight mission. Its primary objectives are technological and strategic, not environmental. Its goals are:

1) Demonstrating human spaceflight capability.

2) Advancing science and technology R&D.

3) Enhancing global collaboration.

Reducing Earth's temperature is NOT an objective of this mission.

Further Insights:

1) Objective: India's first indigenous human spaceflight mission by ISRO.

2) Mission Profile: To send 3 crew members to an orbit of 400 km for 3 days and return them safely to Indian waters.

3) Launch Vehicle: LVM3 (Launch Vehicle Mark-3), colloquially called "Fat Boy".

4) Pre-Flight Test: A female humanoid robot named Vyommitra ("Friend in Sky") will fly first to test life support systems.

Key Terms:

· Pardon: Removes both the sentence and the conviction completely.

· Commutation: Substituting one form of punishment for a lighter form (e.g., death to life imprisonment).

· Remission: Reducing the period of sentence without changing its character (e.g., 2 years to 1 year).

· Respite: Awarding a lesser sentence due to special fact (e.g., pregnancy).

· Reprieve: Stay of execution of a sentence (usually death) for a temporary period.

questions.question: A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech. She said, "I enjoy painting."
questions.questionHtml:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

She said, "I enjoy painting."

options.text: She said that she enjoys painting.
options.html: She said that she enjoys painting.

options.text: She said that she enjoyed painting.
options.html: She said that she enjoyed painting.

options.text: She said she was enjoying painting.
options.html: She said she was enjoying painting.

options.text: She said that she had enjoyed painting.
options.html: She said that she had enjoyed painting.

questions.solution:
The reporting verb said is in the past, so the simple present ("enjoy") is backshifted to simple past ("enjoyed").

This is not a universal truth, so tense change is required.

Why other options are wrong:

1) enjoys incorrectly retains present tense.

3) was enjoying changes the aspect unnecessarily.

4) had enjoyed suggests completed action, which is not intended.

Correct Indirect:

She said that she enjoyed painting.

questions.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph: 1) Overfishing poses a significant threat to global marine ecosystems, leading to the collapse of fish stocks and disrupting the food web. 2) This measure helps to restore fish populations, enhance biodiversity, and ultimately support sustainable fishing practices in adjacent waters. 3) The depletion of key species, such as sharks and tuna, can trigger a cascading effect, with far-reaching consequences for the entire ecosystem. 4) To combat this issue, many governments and conservation organizations have established marine protected areas (MPAs) where fishing is either restricted or prohibited.
questions.questionHtml:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:

1) Overfishing poses a significant threat to global marine ecosystems, leading to the collapse of fish stocks and disrupting the food web.

2) This measure helps to restore fish populations, enhance biodiversity, and ultimately support sustainable fishing practices in adjacent waters.

3) The depletion of key species, such as sharks and tuna, can trigger a cascading effect, with far-reaching consequences for the entire ecosystem.

4) To combat this issue, many governments and conservation organizations have established marine protected areas (MPAs) where fishing is either restricted or prohibited.
questions.solution:
Sentence 1 is the opening sentence because it introduces the main problem: overfishing and its threat.

Sentence 3 logically follows by explaining the consequences of overfishing in detail.

Sentence 4 then presents the solution - marine protected areas.

Sentence 2 concludes by explaining the positive outcomes of this measure, making it a natural ending.

Why other options are wrong:

Other sequences either start with a referential sentence ("This measure") or place the solution before the problem, breaking logical flow.

questions.question: Rearrange the following sentences in correct order to make a logical passage. 1) This involves careful budgeting and debt management. 2) Financial literacy is essential for individual well-being. 3) It empowers people to make informed decisions about money. 4) Education plays a vital role in improving financial literacy rates.
questions.questionHtml:
Rearrange the following sentences in correct order to make a logical passage.

1) This involves careful budgeting and debt management.

2) Financial literacy is essential for individual well-being.

3) It empowers people to make informed decisions about money.

4) Education plays a vital role in improving financial literacy rates.
questions.solution:
Sentence 2 introduces the central idea: financial literacy and its importance.

Sentence 3 logically follows by explaining why it is important (empowerment).

Sentence 1 elaborates on what it involves (budgeting and debt management).

Sentence 4 concludes by stating how it can be improved (through education).

Why other options are wrong:

They either begin with explanation before introducing the topic or disrupt the idea → explanation → details → conclusion structure.

questions.question: Select the correct option for the Direct Speech conversion of the sentence below. He commented that the policy's efficacy would remain conjectural until longitudinal data accrued.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the correct option for the Direct Speech conversion of the sentence below.

He commented that the policy's efficacy would remain conjectural until longitudinal data accrued.

options.text: He commented "The efficacy of the policy remains conjectural as the data are yet to be collected."
options.html: He commented "The efficacy of the policy remains conjectural as the data are yet to be collected."

options.text: He commented, "The policy's efficacy will remain conjectural until longitudinal data accrue."
options.html: He commented, "The policy's efficacy will remain conjectural until longitudinal data accrue."

options.text: He commented, "Until longitudinal data had accrued, the policy's efficacy might have remained conjectural."
options.html: He commented, "Until longitudinal data had accrued, the policy's efficacy might have remained conjectural."

options.text: He commented, "Efficacy remains conjecture till data accumulates."
options.html: He commented, "Efficacy remains conjecture till data accumulates."

questions.solution:
In converting indirect to direct speech, we reverse the tense backshift.

Would remain changes back to will remain, and accrued changes to accrue.

The sentence expresses a future-oriented assessment, so the future tense is retained in direct speech.

Why other options are wrong:

1) remains conjectural changes the tense to present, losing the future sense.

3) Uses had accrued and might have remained, incorrectly shifting to a past hypothetical.

4) Alters wording and meaning, and is not a faithful conversion.

Correct Direct:

He commented, "The policy's efficacy will remain conjectural until longitudinal data accrue."

questions.questionHtml:
Choose the correct form:

The committee, along with its chairperson, ____ scheduled to meet on Monday.
questions.solution:
The subject committee is a collective noun treated as singular here.

The phrase "along with its chairperson" is parenthetical and does not affect verb agreement.

Therefore, the singular verb is is correct.

Why other options are wrong:

1) are treats the subject as plural, which is incorrect here.

3) were changes the tense unnecessarily.

4) have been is both tense- and structure-inappropriate.

Correct Sentence:

The committee, along with its chairperson, is scheduled to meet on Monday.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: They ____ their objections by the time the committee convened.
questions.questionHtml:
Fill in the blank with the correct tense:

They ____ their objections by the time the committee convened.
questions.solution:
The phrase "by the time" followed by a past action requires the past perfect tense for the earlier action.

Thus, had raised correctly shows that the objections were raised before the committee convened.

Why other options are wrong:

1) raised does not show prior completion.

2) have raised is present perfect and incorrect with a past time reference.

3) will raise is future tense and inappropriate.

Correct Sentence:

They had raised their objections by the time the committee convened.

questions.question: According to the passage, how do constraints impact creativity?
questions.questionHtml: According to the passage, how do constraints impact creativity?

options.text: They catalyze creativity by challenging conventional problem-solving.
options.html: They catalyze creativity by challenging conventional problem-solving.

options.text: They make creative thinking predictable and repetitive.
options.html: They make creative thinking predictable and repetitive.

options.text: They increase reliance on external sources.

questions.solution:
The passage explicitly states that innovation often emerges because of constraints, not despite them. Constraints push the mind beyond linear thinking and encourage associative reasoning and metaphorical abstraction, thereby stimulating creativity.

Why other options are wrong:

1) Invariably limit original thinking - The passage argues the opposite.

3) Make creative thinking predictable - Constraints encourage non-linearity, not predictability.

4) Increase reliance on external sources - This is not suggested anywhere in the passage.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about standardized education's effect on creativity?
questions.questionHtml: What does the passage suggest about standardized education's effect on creativity?

options.text: It fosters risk-taking by giving structured guidance.

Why other options are wrong:

1) Fosters risk-taking - The passage says it discourages risk-taking.

2) Ideal environment for innovation - Directly contradicted by the text.

4) Enhances problem-solving through tested frameworks - The passage critiques overreliance on fixed frameworks.

questions.question: What is the closest synonym for "ossified" as used in the line "...about unlearning ossified habits..."?

3) Synthetic - Means artificial or constructed, unrelated here.

4) Tangential - Means indirectly related, not fixed or hardened.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word: CIRCUMSPECT
questions.questionHtml: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word: CIRCUMSPECT

Circumspect means careful, prudent, and mindful of possible risks or consequences. Hence, cautious is the most appropriate synonym.

Option (1) Reckless means careless and rash, which is the opposite.

Option (2) Brash implies aggressive confidence without caution.

Option (3) Carefree suggests lack of concern or worry, not careful judgment.

Usage example:

The manager was circumspect and cautious in approving the deal, rather than reckless or brash.

questions.question: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: Hand and glove
questions.questionHtml:
Choose the correct meaning of idiom:

Hand and glove
questions.solution:
The idiom hand and glove mean working in close association or cooperation, often implying secrecy or mutual benefit.

Options (1), (2), and (4) do not convey closeness or cooperation.

Usage example:

The two officials worked hand and glove, unlike rival departments that acted independently.

questions.question: Find the part of the sentence that contains an error: Neither of the proposed strategies (1)/ seem to address the core issue (2)/ that the committee identified (3)/ during last month's review. (4)/
questions.questionHtml:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

Neither of the proposed strategies (1)/ seem to address the core issue (2)/ that the committee identified (3)/ during last month's review. (4)/
questions.solution:
The subject "Neither of the proposed strategies" is singular, so it requires a singular verb.

Incorrect: seem to address

Correct: seems to address

Options (1), (3), and (4) are grammatically correct.

Corrected sentence:

Neither of the proposed strategies seems to address the core issue that the committee identified during last month's review.

questions.question: Find the part of the sentence that contains an error: The team's objective, despite its vagueness, (1)/ were understood by the evaluators (2)/ to focus more on inclusivity (3)/ than on quantifiable metrics. (4)
questions.questionHtml:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

The team's objective, despite its vagueness, (1)/ were understood by the evaluators (2)/ to focus more on inclusivity (3)/ than on quantifiable metrics. (4)
questions.solution:
The subject of the sentence is "The team's objective", which is singular. Therefore, it must take a singular verb.

Incorrect usage: were understood

Correct usage: was understood

Why other parts are correct:

1) despite its vagueness is a correct parenthetical phrase.

3) to focus more on inclusivity is grammatically correct.

4) than on quantifiable metrics completes the comparison correctly.

Corrected sentence:

The team's objective, despite its vagueness, was understood by the evaluators to focus more on inclusivity than on quantifiable metrics.

questions.question: Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word: The medieval monk copied the codex meticulously.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word:

The medieval monk copied the codex meticulously.

options.text: The scribe placed the codex beside the incunabulum.
options.html: The scribe placed the codex beside the incunabulum.

options.text: The librarian digitized a rare codex from Florence.
options.html: The librarian digitized a rare codex from Florence.

options.text: The AI engineer optimized the codex for faster computation.
options.html: The AI engineer optimized the codex for faster computation.

options.text: The codex was bound in goatskin vellum.
options.html: The codex was bound in goatskin vellum.

questions.solution:
In the given sentence, codex refers to a manuscript or ancient book.

In option (3), codex is used to mean a code or structured set of instructions, giving it a different meaning with the same spelling, thus making it a homonym.

Why other options are wrong:

(1), (2), and (4) all use codex in the manuscript/book sense, same as the original sentence.

Usage example:

The monk preserved a sacred codex, while the programmer debugged a faulty codex.

questions.question: Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence: He is more tall than his brother.
questions.questionHtml:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

He is more tall than his brother.
questions.solution:
For one-syllable adjectives like tall, comparison is formed by adding -er, not by using more.

Hence, taller than is the correct comparative form.

Why other options are wrong:

1) taller to uses the wrong preposition.

2) much taller than changes meaning by adding emphasis.

4) more taller than is a double comparative and incorrect.

Corrected sentence:

He is taller than his brother.

questions.question: Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence: He did not succeed despite of his hard work.
questions.questionHtml: Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence: He did not succeed despite of his hard work.

options.text: in spite of his working hard
options.html: in spite of his working hard

questions.solution:
Despite is a preposition and is not followed by "of."

The correct structure is despite + noun / gerund. Hence, despite his hard work is grammatically correct.

Why other options are wrong:

1) in spite of his working hard is grammatically correct but is wordier and less natural than the given answer.

3) although his hard work is incorrect because although must introduce a clause, not a noun phrase.

4) although he worked hard is grammatically correct but changes the sentence structure instead of merely correcting the error.

Corrected sentence:

He did not succeed despite his hard work.

questions.question: Choose the correct one-word substitution for: 'A place where wild animals are kept'.
questions.questionHtml: Choose the correct one-word substitution for: 'A place where wild animals are kept'.
questions.solution:
A menagerie refers to a collection or place where wild animals are kept, especially for display.

Option (1) Aviary is specifically for birds.

Option (2) Sanctuary is a protected refuge, not primarily for display.

Option (4) Park is a general open area, not a collection of animals.

Usage example:

The royal palace once maintained a menagerie, unlike a sanctuary that focuses on protection rather than exhibition.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word. Obdurate
questions.questionHtml: Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word. Obdurate
questions.solution:
Obdurate means stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action. Its antonym is yielding, which means willing to give way or be flexible.

Option (1) Callous means insensitive, not flexible.

Option (3) Adamant is a synonym of obdurate.

Option (4) Hardened also aligns with rigidity, not softness.

Usage example:

Though he was once obdurate, he later became yielding after hearing reasonable arguments.

questions.question: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: Currying favour
questions.questionHtml:
Choose the correct meaning of idiom:

Currying favour
questions.solution:
Currying favour means attempting to gain someone's approval by excessive praise or flattery, often insincerely.

Option (1) focuses on emotional need, not manipulation.

Option (3) refers to avoidance, not approval-seeking.

Option (4) relates to apology, not flattery.

Usage example:

He tried currying favour with his boss through flattery, instead of earning respect through merit.
